purpose: Source-specific premium teaching replacements authored from the supplied Ralph Loop PDF.
sourceQualification: Examples and templates are instructor-authored reconstructions of mechanisms described in the locally supplied PDF. Product behavior should be checked against current official documentation.

topics.title: Decide when a Ralph loop fits
topics.plainLanguage: A Ralph loop repeatedly gives Claude a bounded unit of work, lets it inspect durable project state, and starts another iteration until an externally visible completion condition is reached. The important decision is not whether the loop sounds powerful; it is whether the work produces reliable evidence on every iteration. Ralph fits tasks such as implementing a list of independent stories, raising test coverage, or validating several technical approaches because files, tests, builds, and task flags expose progress. It is a poor fit for ambiguous taste, one-way production actions, unclear ownership, or work whose success can only be judged after deployment by a person.
topics.mechanism: Pages 7–10 frame Ralph around two recurring problems: long trajectories accumulate misleading context, and an agent may claim completion without satisfying the repository. Repeated fresh iterations reduce trajectory contamination, while durable files carry forward only selected state. This helps only when each iteration can read an explicit objective, choose a small unfinished item, change a reversible workspace, and run a verifier. A completion phrase is never sufficient evidence. The loop controller, repository state, tests, budgets, and approval boundaries form the actual control system.
topics.repositoryScenario: A TypeScript service has twelve migration stories. Each story has acceptance tests, all work occurs in a disposable worktree, and CI-equivalent commands run locally. This is a strong Ralph candidate. A request to ‘make the dashboard feel premium’ has no stable grader and is not. A request to rotate production secrets has irreversible external effects and must remain human-controlled.

workedExample.input: Candidate task: migrate twelve API endpoints from ad-hoc validation to a shared schema. Constraints: preserve response contracts, no production access, one endpoint per task, 20-iteration and 90-minute ceilings.
analysis: Observable output exists: endpoint code, tests, build, and task state.
Work decomposes into independently verifiable stories with a shared contract.
The worktree and Git commits make changes reversible.
No iteration requires an irreversible external action.
A human can review the first iteration before attended execution.
workedExample.decision: Use Ralph after one supervised trial passes. Do not start unattended. Promote only after the same loop selects one task, changes only its scope, runs the complete verifier, records progress, and exits correctly.

topics.weakApproach: Run Claude overnight until the migration is finished. Keep fixing errors and do not stop early.
topics.improvedApproach: In isolated worktree [PATH], process at most one ready task from prd.json per iteration. Preserve response contracts. Run [TEST], [TYPECHECK], and [BUILD]. Mark a task passed only when its acceptance checks succeed. Stop on permission need, repeated identical failure, 20 iterations, 90 minutes, or completion of all tasks. Never access production.
topics.contrastExplanation: The weak request delegates the definition of done, retry policy, scope, and authority. The improved brief supplies observable state, independent verification, reversible execution, explicit budgets, and escalation exits—the conditions that make repetition safer than a long interactive session.
procedure: Write the outcome and list the artifacts that can prove it.
Decompose work into independently verifiable tasks and name their dependencies.
List every external or irreversible action; remove it from the loop or place a human gate before it.
Create an isolated branch/worktree and establish a clean baseline by running the full verifier.
Define completion, iteration, time, cost, repeated-error, permission, and risk stops.
Run exactly one supervised iteration and inspect selection, diff, commands, task update, log, and exit behavior.
Promote to attended execution only after the supervised trace is correct; promote to unattended only after several representative attended runs.

failureModes.symptom: The loop makes aesthetically plausible changes but never converges.
failureModes.cause: Acceptance depends on taste rather than a machine-observable criterion.
failureModes.recovery: Stop the loop, obtain an approved visual reference or human rubric, and return to short attended iterations.

failureModes.symptom: Many tasks change in one iteration and failures cannot be attributed.
failureModes.cause: The task list is not atomic or the prompt permits opportunistic scope expansion.
failureModes.recovery: Restore the last checkpoint, split tasks by independently testable behavior, and enforce one task per iteration.

failureModes.symptom: The loop repeats the same error while spending budget.
failureModes.cause: No repeated-failure detector or escalation condition exists.
failureModes.recovery: Abort after a defined identical error count, preserve logs and diff, then diagnose the blocked assumption interactively.

topics.exercise: Classify five tasks from your repository—dependency upgrade, CSS redesign, test-coverage improvement, production data migration, and API refactor—as Ralph-ready, attended-only, or unsuitable. For each, name the verifier, reversible boundary, human gate, and stop conditions.
masteryRubric: Names at least two direct verifiers for every Ralph-ready task.
Rejects tasks with subjective completion or irreversible ambient authority.
Defines at least five independent stop classes.
Requires a supervised trace before increasing autonomy.
Can explain why fresh iterations plus durable state differ from one long session.

topics.title: Understand the Ralph stop-hook mechanism
topics.plainLanguage: Ralph is a control loop built around Claude Code's attempt to stop. When Claude reaches the end of an iteration, a stop hook examines durable state. If verified work remains, the hook prevents final termination and starts another iteration with the original objective plus current project state. If every task is genuinely verified—or a safety budget says execution must end—the controller allows the session to stop. The hook controls continuation; it does not prove correctness.
topics.mechanism: Pages 11–16 separate three ideas that are easily confused. The stop hook is the continuation mechanism. The repository, task file, and progress log are the state mechanism. The completion promise is a protocol token Claude emits only after its checks say the work is done. A robust controller independently checks task flags, command results, and budgets before trusting that token. This closes a common loophole: a model can sincerely say ‘done’ after checking only the last edit. External state must show that the whole acceptance contract is satisfied.
topics.repositoryScenario: A Python library must make all stories in prd.json pass `pytest`, `ruff check`, and `mypy`. The loop runs one story, records evidence, attempts to stop, and the controller checks whether any task remains unpassed. A failure or unfinished task triggers another bounded iteration; a permission request or exhausted budget exits to a human instead of recycling.

workedExample.input: State before iteration: task API-03 ready, API-01 and API-02 passed, iteration 4/12, elapsed 31/60 minutes.
actions: Claude selects API-03 and changes two files.
`pytest tests/test_api_03.py` passes, but full `mypy` fails in the changed module.
Claude records the failure and attempts to stop without emitting the completion promise.
The hook sees unfinished work and remaining budget, then starts iteration 5 with the failure summary.
If the same mypy error occurs a third time, the repeated-error stop wins and the controller escalates.
workedExample.expectedEvidence: A trace containing selected task, scoped diff, exact command exit codes, updated progress entry, iteration counters, and the controller's continue/stop reason.

topics.weakApproach: Tell Claude: ‘Keep going. When finished, print COMPLETE.’ Accept COMPLETE as proof.
topics.improvedApproach: The controller accepts the completion token only when every required task is passed, the full verification suite exits zero, the worktree is clean except intended changes, and no budget or safety stop fired. Continue only when unfinished work exists and all ceilings remain available.
topics.contrastExplanation: A phrase is model output; completion is repository state plus evidence. The improved controller treats the phrase as a handshake after verification, not the verifier itself, and makes the reason for every continuation or exit inspectable.
procedure: Define the durable state the hook will read: tasks, progress, budgets, and verifier results.
Define mutually exclusive exits: verified completion, continue, budget stop, repeated-error stop, permission stop, and risk escalation.
Make each iteration select at most one ready task and write a completion artifact.
On stop attempt, run or inspect the full required verifier rather than the last narrow test alone.
Allow continuation only when work remains, state is valid, and every budget is below its ceiling.
Log the controller decision and inputs before starting the next iteration.
Test the hook with synthetic complete, incomplete, corrupted-state, repeated-error, and budget-exhausted cases.

failureModes.symptom: The hook loops after all work is complete.
failureModes.cause: Completion state is ambiguous or the controller ignores the full-task predicate.
failureModes.recovery: Stop manually, repair the all-tasks-passed predicate, and add a completed-state hook test.

failureModes.symptom: The hook exits after a narrow test while the build is broken.
failureModes.cause: It trusts the completion promise or last command instead of the complete verification contract.
failureModes.recovery: Reopen the task, require all check exit codes in a structured result, and reject completion when any is absent.

failureModes.symptom: A malformed state file causes unsafe default continuation.
failureModes.cause: The controller fails open.
failureModes.recovery: Fail closed: preserve artifacts, stop, report parse error, and require human repair.

topics.exercise: Draw a state table for six hook inputs: all passed; one ready task; one blocked task; repeated identical error; invalid JSON; iteration limit reached. For each, state the only permitted controller action and the evidence returned to the operator.
masteryRubric: Distinguishes continuation control, durable state, and completion token.
Defines a fail-closed response for invalid state.
Uses the full acceptance contract before accepting completion.
Logs an explicit reason for each transition.
Tests both successful and denied paths.

topics.title: Turn a PRD into atomic prd.json tasks
topics.plainLanguage: The product requirements document explains the outcome and constraints for humans. `prd.json` turns that intent into the small state machine the loop can execute. A task is atomic when one iteration can understand it, change a bounded area, and decide pass or fail using explicit acceptance criteria. Atomic does not mean one file or one function; it means one independently verifiable behavior.
topics.mechanism: Pages 17–23 show a two-stage design. First generate and review the PRD so the product boundary is stable. Then derive prioritized tasks with IDs, descriptions, dependencies, acceptance criteria, and a pass flag. The loop selects a high-priority task whose dependencies have passed. It must not mark the flag from confidence or code appearance: the acceptance evidence determines the transition. Human PRD review prevents an autonomous loop from efficiently implementing the wrong product.
topics.repositoryScenario: Add passwordless email login to an existing web app. The reviewed PRD preserves password login, forbids storing raw tokens, requires expiration and one-time use, and excludes account merging. The executable tasks separate schema, token service, request endpoint, consume endpoint, UI, and end-to-end verification according to dependency order.

workedExample.input: PRD outcome: a registered user can request and consume a 15-minute one-time sign-in link. Non-goals: account merging and removing passwords.

task.title: Consume a one-time login token
acceptance: valid unused token creates a session

workedExample.expectedEvidence: The iteration cites AUTH-02, changes only the token/session path and tests, records both commands and exit codes, and sets passed true only after all four acceptance statements are demonstrated.

topics.weakApproach: Create tasks named ‘backend,’ ‘frontend,’ and ‘testing,’ then let Claude decide when each is done.
topics.improvedApproach: Create behavior-centered tasks with stable IDs, explicit dependencies, observable acceptance statements, exact verification commands, a false initial pass state, and no overlap in ownership. Review the full graph before starting the loop.
topics.contrastExplanation: Layer names hide multiple behaviors and produce late integration surprises. Behavior tasks expose dependencies, keep iterations attributable, and give the controller a reliable state transition. The reviewed PRD protects the loop from solving a locally coherent but globally incorrect problem.
procedure: Write the PRD outcome, user-visible behavior, constraints, non-goals, risks, and global verification suite.
Have a human review ambiguous product and safety decisions before deriving tasks.
List behavior slices and draw their real dependency edges.
For each task, write acceptance criteria that can be observed independently of the implementation.
Attach focused and global verification commands and initialize passed to false.
Check that one normal iteration can finish each task; split tasks that require unrelated changes or separate evidence.
Validate unique IDs, existing dependencies, acyclic ordering, allowed state values, and at least one acceptance criterion before execution.

failureModes.symptom: A task stays active for many iterations and touches unrelated systems.
failureModes.cause: It contains multiple behaviors or hidden dependencies.
failureModes.recovery: Restore the checkpoint, split by independent acceptance evidence, and update downstream dependencies.

failureModes.symptom: All task flags are true but the feature is unusable.
failureModes.cause: Local acceptance omitted a PRD-level integration criterion.
failureModes.recovery: Reopen affected tasks, add an end-to-end acceptance task, and require the global suite before overall completion.

failureModes.symptom: Claude chooses a task whose prerequisite is incomplete.
failureModes.cause: Dependency readiness is prose, not validated state.
failureModes.recovery: Make selection code filter tasks by passed dependencies and reject invalid manual selection.

topics.exercise: Take one feature request from your backlog and produce a one-page PRD plus 5–8 JSON tasks. Exchange it with a reviewer who must identify ambiguous acceptance, overlapping scope, missing dependencies, and claims that cannot be machine-checked.
masteryRubric: PRD separates outcome, constraints, and non-goals.
Every task describes one independently verifiable behavior.
All dependencies resolve and form an acyclic graph.
Pass transitions depend on captured evidence.
A global integration task protects the product-level outcome.

topics.title: Separate progress.txt from durable agents.md knowledge
topics.plainLanguage: A fresh Ralph iteration should not inherit the whole conversation, but it still needs to know what happened. `progress.txt` is the chronological execution journal: task attempted, files changed, commands run, results, and current blocker. `agents.md` is curated project knowledge: stable commands, architectural rules, verified gotchas, and patterns future iterations should follow. One answers ‘what happened recently?’; the other answers ‘what remains true about this project?’
topics.mechanism: Pages 23–27 use files to carry selected memory across fresh iterations. The separation prevents two opposite failures. Without a progress log, the next run repeats investigation and cannot diagnose recurring errors. If every event is promoted to durable instructions, stale attempts and accidental choices pollute future work. Each iteration appends factual execution evidence to progress. Only a discovery that is verified, reusable, and likely to matter beyond the current task is promoted to agents.md. Git remains the authoritative change history; these files explain operational state and learned constraints.
topics.repositoryScenario: During a database migration loop, iteration 3 discovers that integration tests require a disposable PostgreSQL container and that migration filenames must use UTC timestamps. The failed command and container startup belong in progress.txt. The verified naming rule and canonical test command belong in agents.md. A speculative belief that the ORM has a bug belongs in neither until reproduced.

workedExample.progressEntry: Iteration 3 | task DB-02 | changed migrations/20260801_add_status.sql and test | `npm run test:db` failed: connection refused | started documented test container; rerun passed | task remains active pending lint.
workedExample.durableEntry: Database migrations: filenames use UTC `YYYYMMDDHHMM_description.sql`. Verify with `npm run test:db` after starting the disposable database using `docker compose -f compose.test.yml up -d db`.
workedExample.handoff: Iteration 4 reads ready task state, the last relevant progress entries, and the concise durable rule; it does not receive the full prior transcript.

topics.weakApproach: Append every thought, failed hypothesis, and tool dump to agents.md so the next iteration has maximum context.
topics.improvedApproach: Append factual per-iteration evidence to progress.txt. Promote only stable, verified, reusable knowledge to a short categorized agents.md entry. Link to canonical repository documentation rather than duplicating it.
topics.contrastExplanation: Maximum retention is not maximum usefulness. The two-file policy lets the operator reconstruct execution while protecting future decision context from transient noise. Promotion criteria create a deliberate memory boundary.
procedure: Define schemas for progress entries and durable knowledge before running the loop.
At iteration start, read task state, only the relevant recent progress entries, and applicable durable rules.
At iteration end, append task, files, commands, exit results, decision, blocker, and next state to progress.txt.
Ask whether a discovery is verified, reusable across tasks, stable, and not already documented.
If all criteria pass, add or update a concise categorized agents.md rule with its verification command or source path.
Periodically deduplicate, correct, or remove stale durable rules through normal version review.
Keep secrets, raw credentials, huge logs, and unsupported hypotheses out of both files.

failureModes.symptom: Fresh iterations repeat the same failed setup command.
failureModes.cause: Progress omits exact commands/results or is not read during task selection.
failureModes.recovery: Add structured recent-failure retrieval and record the corrected command with evidence.

failureModes.symptom: Agents.md grows into contradictory session history.
failureModes.cause: Transient events are promoted without stability criteria.
failureModes.recovery: Audit entries against repository truth, move historical facts to progress/Git, and retain only verified durable rules.

failureModes.symptom: A stale rule keeps causing bad changes.
failureModes.cause: Durable memory has no owner or review lifecycle.
failureModes.recovery: Correct it in a focused commit, link the change that invalidated it, and add instruction review to relevant PRs.

topics.exercise: Given ten notes from a failed feature iteration, classify each as task state, progress evidence, durable knowledge, canonical documentation, or discard. Write one valid progress entry and one valid durable rule, then explain why the remaining notes were not promoted.
masteryRubric: Progress entries reconstruct actions and observed results.
Durable entries contain only verified reusable rules.
Neither file stores secrets or raw transcript dumps.
A fresh iteration receives enough state without prior conversation.
Stale knowledge has a versioned correction path.

topics.title: Build feedback channels into every Ralph iteration
topics.plainLanguage: A Ralph loop improves only when the environment answers its actions. The prompt supplies intent, but tests, lint, type checks, builds, task state, Git, and curated memory tell the next iteration what actually happened. A feedback channel is useful when its result is captured, attributed to the current change, and converted into an explicit next-state decision. Merely running a command is not feedback if its output disappears or is ignored.
topics.mechanism: Pages 27–30 describe an iteration as a closed evidence loop. Task state selects work; focused checks provide fast local evidence; the global suite detects integration damage; Git reveals scope; progress records the trace; durable knowledge prevents repeated mistakes. These channels have different strength and cost. Run inexpensive focused checks early, then the full contract before marking the task passed. The next iteration should receive a concise failure summary and artifact paths, not an unbounded terminal transcript.
topics.repositoryScenario: A Go service loop implements one rate-limit story. Unit tests pass, but `go test ./...` exposes a race in another package and `git diff --stat` shows an unexpected generated file. The task remains active. The iteration records both failures, removes the unrelated file, repairs the race, and only then advances task state.

feedbackOrder: Read prd.json and select one dependency-ready task.
Run the focused test once to establish or reproduce the starting signal.
Make the minimal change and rerun focused tests.
Run the repository-level suite required by the PRD.
Inspect diff/status for scope and generated artifacts.
Write structured results to progress and transition task state.
workedExample.expectedEvidence: A machine-readable summary containing command, exit code, duration, artifact/log path, expected predicate, observed result, and final task transition.

topics.weakApproach: After editing, run whatever tests seem relevant. If output looks good, mark the task done and let the next iteration handle problems.
topics.improvedApproach: Define a fixed evidence ladder per task: focused behavior check, static checks, global suite, diff/scope inspection, then state transition. Capture every result and keep the task unpassed if any required channel is absent or fails.
topics.contrastExplanation: The improved loop prevents verifier shopping and missing-output optimism. A predeclared evidence ladder makes each transition reproducible and lets later iterations distinguish product failure, tooling failure, scope failure, and stale state.
procedure: For each task, name focused checks and inherited PRD-level checks.
Define the expected predicate for every command, including artifacts beyond exit zero.
Establish a baseline so pre-existing failures are distinguishable from regressions.
Run focused feedback after the smallest meaningful edit, then broader checks.
Capture command, result, duration, and log path in structured iteration output.
Inspect Git diff/status and reject unrelated scope even when tests pass.
Transition task state only after all required channels report acceptable evidence; pass concise failures to the next iteration.

failureModes.symptom: The loop repeatedly fixes one test while breaking another.
failureModes.cause: It runs only focused checks and omits the global contract.
failureModes.recovery: Reopen the task, establish the full-suite baseline, and require global success before pass.

failureModes.symptom: Logs consume context and obscure the actual error.
failureModes.cause: Raw output is copied into the next prompt.
failureModes.recovery: Persist full logs as artifacts and pass a structured summary plus relevant excerpt and path.

failureModes.symptom: A command exits zero but the required artifact is missing.
failureModes.cause: The verifier checks process success rather than the behavioral predicate.
failureModes.recovery: Add artifact/content assertions and treat absent evidence as failure.

topics.exercise: Design an evidence ladder for one repository story. Include a focused test, static check, global check, runtime or artifact assertion, and diff inspection. Inject one known failure at each layer and confirm the state machine refuses to mark the task passed.
masteryRubric: Every acceptance claim maps to a direct feedback channel.
Focused and global checks serve distinct purposes.
Full logs are preserved without flooding the next context.
Scope inspection can fail a task even when tests pass.
Task transitions are reproducible from captured evidence.

topics.title: Earn progression from supervised to unattended Ralph loops
topics.plainLanguage: Ralph autonomy is a promotion ladder, not a switch. Level 1 is one supervised iteration: a person watches selection, edits, verification, state update, and exit. Level 2 is an attended multi-iteration loop: the controller repeats bounded work while a person remains available and reviews checkpoints. Level 3 is unattended execution: the operator may leave, so isolation, budgets, observability, deterministic checks, and emergency stop must carry the safety burden. Success at a lower level is evidence required for promotion, not a guarantee.
topics.mechanism: Pages 30–43 combine technical budgets with three maturity levels. Iteration, elapsed-time, cost, repeated-error, permission, and risk limits are independent; whichever fires first stops execution. Promotion requires representative traces showing correct task selection, bounded diffs, verifier behavior, state integrity, and clean exits. Unattended execution also needs credential minimization, network restrictions, recoverable checkpoints, remote visibility, and a fail-closed controller. The loop should be demoted after verifier drift, task-schema changes, new external authority, or repeated recovery events.
topics.repositoryScenario: A monorepo team wants an overnight test-repair loop. They first run five supervised single-test fixes. Next they run a 30-minute attended loop capped at four tasks. Only after clean traces do they permit an isolated overnight run with no production credentials, eight iterations, a two-hour limit, a cost ceiling, three-identical-error abort, branch-only writes, and morning review before merge.

workedExample.level1Gate: One task; operator watches; all commands and state transitions correct; stop paths manually exercised.
workedExample.level2Gate: Several representative tasks; bounded polling; checkpoint after each task; operator can interrupt; no scope or state corruption.
workedExample.level3Gate: Isolated environment; least privilege; independent budgets; remote heartbeat; emergency stop; artifacts retained; no external irreversible effects; human review before integration.
workedExample.demotionRule: Any invalid state transition, missing log, repeated identical failure beyond threshold, unplanned external access, or unreliable verifier returns the workflow to Level 1.

topics.weakApproach: The first iteration worked, so run the same prompt overnight with dangerous permission bypass and check the result tomorrow.
topics.improvedApproach: Use explicit promotion evidence. Increase duration and task count gradually; do not increase permissions unless the task requires them. Run unattended only in isolation with independent ceilings, heartbeat, abort path, retained traces, and review-before-merge.
topics.contrastExplanation: A correct happy path says little about failure behavior. The promotion ladder tests the control system under realistic work and denied paths. Isolation and budgets limit consequences when the model, task state, verifier, dependency, or environment behaves unexpectedly.
procedure: Define required traces and promotion criteria before the Level 1 trial.
Run several supervised iterations spanning success, test failure, blocked dependency, and stop conditions.
Review diffs, logs, state transitions, and budget accounting; repair the harness rather than prompt around structural failures.
Run a short attended loop with strict task/iteration/time ceilings and exercise manual cancellation.
Threat-model unattended authority: filesystem, credentials, network, package installation, external services, and integration.
Configure independent budgets, heartbeat, emergency stop, artifact retention, and fail-closed invalid-state behavior.
Promote only after representative evidence; review every unattended result before merge and demote when the contract changes.

failureModes.symptom: Overnight execution spends hours repeating one dependency error.
failureModes.cause: Only iteration/time limits exist; repeated identical failures are not classified.
failureModes.recovery: Terminate, preserve traces, add error fingerprint threshold, and return to supervised diagnosis.

failureModes.symptom: A loop modifies files outside task ownership.
failureModes.cause: Isolation exists but write scope is broad and diff scope is not a gate.
failureModes.recovery: Discard unauthorized changes, constrain workspace/permissions, add path allowlist and diff gate, demote to Level 1.

failureModes.symptom: The operator cannot tell whether a remote loop is alive or safe.
failureModes.cause: No heartbeat, structured status, or emergency stop.
failureModes.recovery: Stop the host/session through the containment boundary; require visibility and cancellation before another attended run.

topics.exercise: Create a promotion checklist for one repeatable repository job. Run a Level 1 trial with an intentionally failing test and a malformed task-state copy. Demonstrate that both stop safely. Design, but do not run, Level 3 permissions, budgets, heartbeat, and review gate.
masteryRubric: Defines distinct evidence gates for all three levels.
Uses independent time, iteration, cost, error, permission, and risk stops.
Unattended work is isolated and lacks unnecessary credentials.
Emergency stop and artifact recovery are tested.
Workflow is demoted when assumptions or authority change.

topics.title: Choose Ralph patterns by the kind of evidence you need
topics.plainLanguage: The Ralph article presents four application patterns, each with a different unit of work and success signal. Feature builder completes scoped product stories. Test-until-green adds or repairs tests in small attributable units. Multi-persona review gathers several role-based critiques; it broadens perspectives but is not independent truth because the same model family and context may share blind spots. Proof-of-concept validator reduces uncertainty with disposable experiments rather than production-quality code. Choosing the pattern first prevents one generic loop from mixing delivery, evaluation, and exploration.
topics.mechanism: Pages 43–53 vary the loop contract rather than merely the prompt wording. Feature work advances PRD task state and requires behavior plus regression evidence. Test work advances a coverage or failure target while guarding against implementation-mirroring assertions. Persona review produces findings, evidence, severity, and disposition—not code by default. A POC answers a named feasibility question under a time box and records what was learned, including negative results. Patterns can be sequenced: run POC before committing architecture, build the chosen feature, improve tests, then conduct fresh review. Their artifacts and stop predicates must remain separate.
topics.repositoryScenario: A team is considering WebSocket notifications. First run a POC loop to test proxy compatibility and reconnect behavior. If feasible, convert findings into reviewed feature tasks and run feature-builder iterations. Run test-until-green for reconnection edge cases. Finish with security, reliability, and maintainability personas that cite the diff; a human disposition decides fixes.

workedExample.featureBuilder: Input: one ready story. Evidence: acceptance tests, full suite, focused diff, passed task flag. Stop: all stories verified or boundary hit.
workedExample.testUntilGreen: Input: named uncovered behavior or failing test. Evidence: observed red test, meaningful assertion, green focused/global suite, coverage delta where useful. Stop: target reached without production-behavior distortion.
workedExample.multiPersonaReview: Input: frozen diff and requirements. Evidence: each persona cites file/line, reproduction, impact, and confidence; duplicates merged; human dispositions recorded. Stop: all review lenses complete, not ‘no findings.’
workedExample.pocValidator: Input: one uncertainty and decision threshold. Evidence: disposable experiment, measurements/logs, limitations, and recommendation. Stop: question answered, time box exhausted, or blocking dependency identified.
workedExample.sequence: POC → feature builder → test-until-green → fresh review; never let POC shortcuts silently become production architecture.

topics.weakApproach: Ask four personas to build, test, review, and redesign the feature simultaneously until they all agree it is production ready.
topics.improvedApproach: Select one pattern per stage, freeze its input, define its artifact and verifier, and complete its handoff before the next pattern. Use an independent human or separate evaluation system for final decisions; treat persona agreement as breadth, not proof.
topics.contrastExplanation: Mixed roles share mutable state and redefine success while working. Separated patterns preserve attribution: the POC answers feasibility, the builder changes behavior, the tester challenges it, and the reviewer reports risks. Explicit handoffs prevent experimental shortcuts and self-review confidence from masquerading as verification.
procedure: Name the current uncertainty: feasibility, delivery, test signal, or review risk.
Choose the single pattern whose artifact directly reduces that uncertainty.
Freeze the input contract and define the unit of work, allowed changes, evidence, budgets, and stop predicate.
Run one supervised iteration and inspect whether it produced the intended artifact rather than drifting into another role.
Complete the pattern's artifact and record limitations before handing off.
If sequencing patterns, translate evidence into the next input; do not carry raw conversational trajectory.
Require independent disposition/review before integrating production changes, especially after persona review or a POC.

failureModes.symptom: A POC accumulates abstractions and is merged as production code.
failureModes.cause: The experiment lacks a disposable boundary and explicit handoff.
failureModes.recovery: Extract findings, discard or quarantine the spike, and create production tasks with normal quality gates.

failureModes.symptom: Coverage rises but tests pass incorrect implementations.
failureModes.cause: Test iterations mirror current code rather than user-visible contracts.
failureModes.recovery: Write a failing behavior example first, add mutation/negative cases, and have a fresh reviewer challenge assertion value.

failureModes.symptom: All personas agree and a serious defect remains.
failureModes.cause: Shared model/context creates correlated review blind spots.
failureModes.recovery: Use independent runtime evidence and human/external review; record persona review as advisory findings only.

failureModes.symptom: Feature iterations continually redesign architecture.
failureModes.cause: Feasibility uncertainty was not isolated before delivery.
failureModes.recovery: Pause builder, run a time-boxed POC for the disputed assumption, review evidence, then re-plan tasks.

topics.exercise: Take a proposed caching feature and write four separate one-iteration contracts: POC for invalidation feasibility, feature story for one cache path, test target for stale-data behavior, and reliability review. Specify artifact, verifier, stop, and handoff for each, then order them and justify the order.
masteryRubric: Selects a pattern from the uncertainty, not personal preference.
Each pattern has a distinct artifact and success predicate.
POC code is explicitly disposable or promoted through normal engineering gates.
Tests challenge behavior rather than mirror implementation.
Persona review is labeled advisory and receives independent disposition.
Pattern handoffs contain evidence and limitations without raw trajectory.

topics.title: Use CLAUDE.md as project memory, boundary, and primer
topics.plainLanguage: CLAUDE.md is durable project context that Claude Code loads automatically. It should teach stable facts needed across many tasks: what the repository is, how to work in it, and which boundaries must not be crossed. It is not a task backlog, chat transcript, or substitute for discoverable code and normal documentation. The masterclass describes it as memory, boundary, and primer; official guidance emphasizes concise, specific instructions that are reviewed like code.
topics.mechanism: Automatic loading makes every line consume attention on every applicable session. High-value entries prevent repeated discovery or recurring mistakes: canonical commands, architecture boundaries, generated-file warnings, test expectations, and pointers to deeper documents. Low-value narrative competes with the current task and becomes dangerous when stale. Instructions influence behavior but do not technically enforce policy; hooks, permissions, CI, and review must enforce deterministic requirements.
topics.repositoryScenario: In a TypeScript monorepo, the root file explains the product, package map, package manager, global checks, and prohibition on editing generated clients. Package-specific rules live nearer each package. A temporary OAuth feature plan remains in PLAN.md, not CLAUDE.md.

workedExample.weak: This is a modern app. Write clean code and test carefully.
workedExample.improved: Purpose: multi-tenant billing. Packages: apps/api, apps/web, packages/contracts. Use pnpm. Before completion run pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test. Never edit packages/contracts/generated; run pnpm generate:contracts. See docs/architecture.md for boundaries.
workedExample.evidence: A fresh session can locate entry points, run the correct checks, and avoid the generated directory without receiving feature-specific noise.

topics.weakApproach: Store every preference, past failure, task note, and documentation page in the root CLAUDE.md.
topics.improvedApproach: Store only stable, recurring, repository-specific guidance; link deeper material; enforce invariants outside prose; keep task state in task artifacts.
topics.contrastExplanation: Automatic context has a recurring cost. Concision improves signal, and separating advisory instructions from enforcement prevents false safety confidence.
procedure: Map repository purpose, structure, canonical commands, and non-obvious boundaries.
Keep only facts likely to affect many future tasks.
Replace vague style advice with observable commands or repository examples.
Link detailed architecture and workflow documents instead of copying them.
Move temporary plans and progress out of CLAUDE.md.
Back deterministic rules with hooks, permissions, tests, or CI.
Ask a fresh session to explain the file and verify every claim against the repository.

failureModes.symptom: Claude follows an obsolete command.
failureModes.cause: The file changed independently of scripts.
failureModes.recovery: Correct it in the same PR as the command change and add instruction review.

failureModes.symptom: Critical rules are ignored.
failureModes.cause: The file is long and contradictory or relies on prose enforcement.
failureModes.recovery: Prune, scope narrowly, and enforce the invariant mechanically.

topics.exercise: Audit an existing CLAUDE.md. Mark each line stable, task-specific, duplicated, vague, or enforceable. Produce a concise replacement and test it with a fresh repository-orientation prompt.
masteryRubric: Purpose and repository map are concrete.
Commands exist and run.
Boundaries name exact paths or behaviors.
Temporary material is excluded.
Machine-enforceable rules have an enforcement path.

topics.title: Create and bootstrap CLAUDE.md safely
topics.plainLanguage: A useful CLAUDE.md is discovered from the repository, not invented from a framework stereotype. The masterclass presents generated initialization, manual authoring, and incremental memory capture. Generation is fast but must be audited; manual authoring is controlled but may omit hidden conventions; incremental capture is accurate to lived work but can become a pile of anecdotes. A strong bootstrap combines all three.
topics.mechanism: Repository inspection supplies evidence: manifests identify commands, CI identifies required checks, entry points reveal architecture, existing docs state intent, and recent diffs reveal conventions. Generated claims remain hypotheses until a file or successful command supports them. Start small so errors do not become automatically loaded misinformation, then add only repeated discoveries.
topics.repositoryScenario: A maintainer inherits a Python service. Claude inspects pyproject.toml, Makefile, CI, src layout, migrations, and tests; drafts a 45-line file; the maintainer runs every command and removes a guessed Docker workflow not used by CI.

workedExample.input: Unknown repository with README, pyproject.toml, Makefile, .github/workflows/test.yml, src/, tests/.
workedExample.evidence: Every operational statement links to a repository file or observed command result.

topics.weakApproach: Run an initializer, accept its output, and treat it as authoritative.
topics.improvedApproach: Generate a draft, require file-backed citations, execute claimed commands, human-review boundaries, and commit a minimal verified version.
topics.contrastExplanation: Generation accelerates discovery but cannot distinguish conventions from guesses without repository evidence and execution.
procedure: Inspect manifests, CI, docs, entry points, tests, and generated paths.
Draft purpose, map, commands, and boundaries with source paths.
Delete generic advice and unsupported claims.
Run each command from a clean checkout or equivalent baseline.
Review security and ownership boundaries with a maintainer.
Commit the smallest useful file.
Capture later recurring discoveries through reviewed changes, not ad-hoc accumulation.

failureModes.symptom: The bootstrap names nonexistent commands.
failureModes.cause: Generated inference was not executed.
failureModes.recovery: Remove or correct it from manifests/CI and record the observed result.

failureModes.symptom: Important conventions are absent.
failureModes.cause: Only top-level files were inspected.
failureModes.recovery: Add narrowly scoped instructions when real work exposes a repeated rule.

topics.exercise: Bootstrap instructions for a small repository, attach evidence for every line, and have a second person invalidate at least one unsupported assumption before merge.
masteryRubric: Every claim is file-backed or command-verified.
No generic filler remains.
Commands are runnable.
Human review covers risky boundaries.
The initial file is concise and versioned.

topics.title: Organize CLAUDE.md as why, how, and what
topics.plainLanguage: WHY explains the product purpose and architectural intent. HOW gives canonical commands and operational procedure. WHAT maps the repository and points to important locations. This order lets Claude interpret a task before choosing actions: purpose constrains tradeoffs, commands make work reproducible, and the map prevents blind file search.
topics.mechanism: Pages 11–15 use the three-part structure to keep unlike information separated. WHY should be short and decision-relevant, not marketing copy. HOW should contain copy-safe commands plus when to use them. WHAT should orient rather than enumerate every file. Clear Markdown headings make information retrievable and expose omissions during review.
topics.repositoryScenario: For a payments service, WHY states tenant isolation and auditability; HOW lists local setup, focused tests, full checks, migrations, and generated-client refresh; WHAT maps API, domain, persistence, contracts, and tests.

workedExample.why: Multi-tenant billing; tenant isolation and auditable ledger history outrank convenience.
workedExample.how: Use pnpm. Focused: pnpm test -- [path]. Full: pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test. Generate contracts with pnpm generate:contracts.
workedExample.what: apps/api routes; packages/billing domain; packages/db persistence; packages/contracts generated boundary; tests/e2e system behavior.

topics.weakApproach: Mix purpose, file lists, temporary notes, and commands in one long bullet list.
topics.improvedApproach: Use concise WHY/HOW/WHAT sections, with deeper links and exact commands.
topics.contrastExplanation: The structured version lets an agent answer intent, operation, and location separately and makes stale facts easier to find.
procedure: Write one paragraph explaining decisions the product purpose should influence.
List canonical setup and verification commands with conditions.
Map major components, entry points, tests, and generated boundaries.
Remove exhaustive file inventories.
Link deeper architecture or runbooks.
Test orientation with a fresh session.
Revise any answer that required hidden human knowledge.

failureModes.symptom: Claude follows architecture mechanically without product intent.
failureModes.cause: WHY is absent or promotional.
failureModes.recovery: Add decision-relevant invariants and tradeoffs.

failureModes.symptom: The map is instantly stale.
failureModes.cause: WHAT lists individual files.
failureModes.recovery: Map stable components and link a generated index.

topics.exercise: Rewrite ten mixed instructions into WHY/HOW/WHAT, then ask a fresh session where to change one behavior, how to verify it, and which invariant constrains the design.
masteryRubric: WHY affects a real design decision.
HOW commands are executable.
WHAT maps stable components.
Detailed docs are linked, not duplicated.
Fresh-session answers are file-backed.

topics.title: Place instructions at the narrowest stable scope
topics.plainLanguage: Instruction hierarchy lets global preferences, repository rules, and directory-specific conventions coexist. A rule should live at the narrowest scope where it is always true. Root rules apply broadly; nested files specialize work in a package or directory. Broad placement wastes context and can make a correct rule wrong elsewhere.
topics.mechanism: Pages 8–10 illustrate hierarchical loading. In a monorepo, root instructions define shared commands and boundaries; `apps/web/CLAUDE.md` may define UI tests; `services/payments/CLAUDE.md` may define ledger invariants. Narrow files reduce conditional prose and allow ownership near the code. Conflicts require a documented precedence model and testing in the actual working directory.
topics.repositoryScenario: The root requires pnpm and global checks. The web package requires accessibility tests and component conventions. The payments service forbids destructive migration edits. Placing all three at root would send irrelevant UI detail into backend work and risk applying migration rules to unrelated packages.

workedExample.root: Shared package manager, repository map, global checks, generated-file rule.
workedExample.web: Component locations, browser test command, accessibility gate.
workedExample.payments: Ledger invariant, migration workflow, service-specific integration test.
workedExample.evidence: Sessions started in each scope explain only applicable rules and select correct commands.

topics.weakApproach: Put every team convention in the root file with many ‘if working in…’ paragraphs.
topics.improvedApproach: Keep shared truth at root and place package rules beside their owned code; document precedence and test loading.
topics.contrastExplanation: Locality reduces irrelevant context, conditional ambiguity, and ownership drift while preserving shared constraints.
procedure: Inventory instructions and mark their true scope.
Keep universally applicable rules at root.
Create nested files for stable package-specific differences.
Remove duplicated parent rules unless a local exception is explicit.
Name owners for specialized instructions.
Test representative sessions in each directory.
Review hierarchy when packages move or ownership changes.

failureModes.symptom: Backend work follows frontend conventions.
failureModes.cause: A local rule is stored globally.
failureModes.recovery: Move it to the frontend scope and test loading.

failureModes.symptom: Nested instructions contradict root silently.
failureModes.cause: Exception and precedence are undocumented.
failureModes.recovery: State the exception explicitly, remove duplication, and add an instruction-loading check.

topics.exercise: Classify fifteen repository rules as global, root, package, path-specific, or task-specific; create a three-file hierarchy and test it from two working directories.
masteryRubric: Every rule lives where it is consistently true.
Shared rules are not duplicated.
Exceptions are explicit.
Owners and review triggers exist.
Loading behavior is tested.

topics.title: Reveal detailed instructions only when needed
topics.plainLanguage: Progressive disclosure keeps automatically loaded instructions short and links to detailed guidance that is opened only for a relevant task. The root file becomes an index of stable rules and triggers, while `agent_docs` or normal documentation holds migration procedures, deployment runbooks, and architecture detail.
topics.mechanism: Pages 15–21 argue that less automatic context can improve instruction adherence. A useful link states when to read the target, not merely its filename. The agent loads database migration guidance when a migration is involved, not during a CSS change. Conditional retrieval must remain reliable: critical safety rules cannot be hidden behind a link the agent may never open and should be enforced mechanically.
topics.repositoryScenario: Root instructions say: ‘For schema or migration work, read agent_docs/database-migrations.md before editing.’ The linked guide contains naming, expand/migrate/contract steps, rollback, and test commands. UI work never loads it.

workedExample.before: A 700-line root file containing deployment, database, UI, API, security, and release manuals.
workedExample.after: A 70-line root with invariants, commands, map, and conditional links to five owned documents.
workedExample.test: Fresh sessions for migration and UI tasks load different working sets and both retain global safety boundaries.

topics.weakApproach: Preload every document so Claude cannot miss anything.
topics.improvedApproach: Keep global invariants visible; provide descriptive conditional links; verify retrieval and enforce critical rules outside prose.
topics.contrastExplanation: More context can bury the applicable rule. Selective loading improves signal without abandoning traceable detail.
procedure: Measure and classify root content by frequency and scope.
Retain universal high-impact rules.
Move long conditional procedures into owned documents.
Add links that state the triggering task or path.
Keep critical deny rules visible and mechanically enforced.
Test retrieval with representative tasks and a fresh session.
Review links and owners when workflows change.

failureModes.symptom: Claude misses a required runbook.
failureModes.cause: The link has no trigger or is buried.
failureModes.recovery: Write an explicit task/path condition and add a workflow check.

failureModes.symptom: A linked document is stale.
failureModes.cause: It lacks ownership and version review.
failureModes.recovery: Correct it with the workflow change and assign an owner.

topics.exercise: Reduce a long root instruction file by at least half without losing any global invariant. Create conditional documents and prove two task prompts load the correct distinct detail.
masteryRubric: Root context is concise.
Links state when they apply.
Critical safety is not optional retrieval.
Linked material has owners.
Representative retrieval tests succeed.

topics.title: Encode repeatable workflows as ordered, verifiable procedures
topics.plainLanguage: A workflow instruction tells Claude how this repository repeatedly performs an operation: preconditions, ordered actions, checks, approvals, and recovery. It is stronger than ‘follow our migration process’ because every transition and success signal is visible.
topics.mechanism: Page 29 recommends encoding recurring workflows. Good workflow prose behaves like an executable checklist while remaining readable: it names input, scope, commands, expected artifacts, stop points, and rollback. Commands should be copied from repository truth and deterministic portions should migrate to scripts or hooks. Human judgment remains at ambiguous or irreversible gates.
topics.repositoryScenario: A database migration workflow requires a clean worktree, expand-only schema change, generated client refresh, focused and integration tests, rollback notes, and DBA approval before production application.

workedExample.trigger: Any change under db/migrations or schema definitions.
steps: Stop for approval before external application.
workedExample.evidence: Migration file, regenerated client diff, passing command outputs, rollback note, approval record.

topics.weakApproach: When changing the database, be careful and test everything.
topics.improvedApproach: Define trigger, preconditions, exact sequence, checks, artifacts, approval boundary, and recovery; point to the canonical script.
topics.contrastExplanation: The improved workflow is reproducible and reviewable; the weak statement delegates essential repository knowledge to guesswork.
procedure: Choose one recurring failure-prone operation.
Document trigger and preconditions.
List the smallest ordered actions and exact commands.
Name artifacts and acceptance evidence.
Place approval before irreversible transitions.
Document rollback and escalation.
Test the procedure, then automate deterministic portions.

failureModes.symptom: Steps run out of order.
failureModes.cause: Dependencies are implicit.
failureModes.recovery: Number transitions and attach prerequisites.

failureModes.symptom: Workflow says complete without evidence.
failureModes.cause: Checks and artifacts are unnamed.
failureModes.recovery: Add exact predicates and capture outputs.

topics.exercise: Convert one tribal workflow into a seven-part procedure and have a fresh session execute it in a disposable branch while an observer records ambiguities.
masteryRubric: Trigger and preconditions are explicit.
Order reflects real dependencies.
Commands and artifacts are exact.
Approval precedes irreversible action.
Recovery is actionable.

topics.title: Apply special rules only under the right condition
topics.plainLanguage: Conditional instructions activate only for a relevant file path, task type, environment, or tool. They keep exceptional rules from polluting ordinary work and make the trigger reviewable. A condition must be objective enough that two people agree when it applies.
topics.mechanism: Pages 29–32 discuss context-specific guidance. Conditions may refer to paths such as migrations, tasks such as release preparation, or environments such as production. The instruction must state trigger, required reading/action, and exit. Environment-sensitive work also needs permission enforcement; prose alone cannot prevent a production command.
topics.repositoryScenario: When files under `infra/terraform/**` change, read the infrastructure guide, run format/validate/plan, save the plan artifact, and stop for platform-team approval. Ordinary application edits do not load these rules.

workedExample.required: Read agent_docs/terraform.md; run terraform fmt -check and validate; create plan with approved workspace.
workedExample.evidence: Saved plan artifact and approval request.

topics.weakApproach: Use infrastructure best practices when relevant.
topics.improvedApproach: Define an observable trigger, exact procedure, forbidden transition, verifier, and approver.
topics.contrastExplanation: Objective triggers eliminate guesswork and keep exceptional context narrow; technical enforcement protects the deny boundary.
procedure: Identify a rule that is wrong or noisy outside a narrow case.
Choose a path/task/tool/environment predicate.
State required document and actions.
State checks, forbidden operations, and exit.
Back sensitive denial with permissions/hooks.
Test positive and negative trigger cases.
Version the condition with the governed workflow.

failureModes.symptom: Rules load for unrelated work.
failureModes.cause: The trigger uses vague semantics.
failureModes.recovery: Replace it with an observable path/task predicate.

failureModes.symptom: Production apply occurs despite prose.
failureModes.cause: A deny rule is not enforced.
failureModes.recovery: Revoke authority, require approval, and enforce the command boundary.

topics.exercise: Write one path rule and one environment rule. Test applicable and non-applicable tasks and demonstrate the prohibited action is mechanically denied.
masteryRubric: Trigger is objective.
Positive and negative paths are tested.
Procedure and verifier are named.
Sensitive denies are enforced.
Rules remain narrow.

topics.title: Maintain CLAUDE.md as versioned code
topics.plainLanguage: CLAUDE.md affects every applicable session, so stale instructions are production defects in the development workflow. Maintain it through normal version control: review changes, connect updates to the repository change that requires them, assign ownership, and periodically test whether a fresh session can follow it.
topics.mechanism: Pages 36–38 recommend treating instructions as code. Maintenance has event-driven triggers—command, architecture, ownership, path, generated boundary, or workflow changes—and periodic review for accumulated noise. Diffs expose why a rule changed and allow rollback. Discoveries should be generalized and verified before promotion; one unusual incident should not become a universal rule.
topics.repositoryScenario: A PR replaces Jest with Vitest. The same PR updates canonical commands, removes Jest-specific troubleshooting, changes nested UI instructions, and runs a fresh-session orientation check. CODEOWNERS requests developer-experience review.

workedExample.change: pnpm test now invokes Vitest and snapshots move directories.
workedExample.instructionDiff: Update HOW command and UI snapshot path; remove obsolete Jest flag.
workedExample.validation: Clean checkout command passes; fresh session selects Vitest; no stale Jest text remains.
workedExample.history: Commit message links instruction change to test migration.

topics.weakApproach: Update CLAUDE.md occasionally when someone notices Claude behaving strangely.
topics.improvedApproach: Define change triggers, ownership, PR review, executable checks, freshness audits, and a deletion policy.
topics.contrastExplanation: Reactive maintenance lets incorrect automatic context cause repeated failures. Lifecycle ownership makes instruction drift visible at the change that creates it.
procedure: Assign owners for root and nested instruction files.
Add instruction review to changes in commands, architecture, paths, workflows, or policy.
Verify changed commands from a clean baseline.
Review instruction diffs like code for scope and contradictions.
Test orientation and one representative workflow with fresh context.
Schedule periodic prune/link/staleness audits.
Delete obsolete rules and record the reason in version history.

failureModes.symptom: Sessions repeatedly use a removed tool.
failureModes.cause: Tool migration did not trigger instruction review.
failureModes.recovery: Correct all scopes, verify commands, and add a PR checklist trigger.

failureModes.symptom: The file grows after every incident.
failureModes.cause: No promotion or deletion criteria.
failureModes.recovery: Require recurrence, stability, evidence, and correct scope; prune anecdotes.

topics.exercise: Choose a recent repository change and audit every instruction it invalidated. Prepare a focused instruction diff, verification transcript, owner review, and deletion rationale.
masteryRubric: Owners and update triggers exist.
Instruction changes travel with repository changes.
Commands are clean-baseline verified.
Fresh-session behavior is tested.
Obsolete guidance is deleted, not merely superseded.
